qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: A science-fair judge discovers that one finalist is her neighbor's daughter. She says nothing to the organizers, studies every project closely, and fills out the official rubric for each -- but then quietly adds two extra points to the girl's total, points no rubric line awards. Which description best fits the judge?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: Careless, since she barely glances at each project before scribbling down a score.
Impartial, since she scores every finalist with the very same official rubric.
Biased, since she quietly tilts the result toward the one finalist she knows.
Indecisive, since she simply cannot make up her mind about who deserves to win.

qti-content-body.p: Correct. The judge did everything by the book until the end -- then slipped her neighbor's daughter two points that no rubric line awards, and told no one about the connection. Quietly tilting a result toward someone you favor is bias, no matter how carefully the rest of the scoring was done.

Follow the two extra points. The judge studies every project closely, so she is not careless; she reaches her scores without hesitation, so she is not indecisive; and a judge who slips unearned points to someone she knows is favoring a side -- precisely what an impartial judge never does. Which word names a judge who tilts the outcome toward a favorite?

Careless would mean rushing -- barely glancing before scribbling a score. This judge studies every project closely and completes the full rubric for each one. Her scoring is attentive; the problem lies in what she adds after the rubric is done.

Impartial means favoring no one -- and for most of her scoring, the rubric kept her honest. But two extra points that no rubric line awards, given only to her neighbor's daughter and hidden from the organizers, is favoritism by definition. One quiet thumb on the scale is all it takes: a judge who tilts toward anyone is biased, not impartial.

Indecisive would mean she cannot settle on scores at all. She settles on them without any trouble -- every rubric is filled out and every total turned in. The flaw is in whose total she quietly padded, not in any struggle to decide.
